title: Like the earth
hookLine: the God-conscious one is like the earth, dug by some, anointed by others, the same to both

lines: A PLOW, A WELL, A GRAVE.
THE EARTH DOES THE SAME THING.
cards: Stand in a field and think about what the ground under your feet puts up with. A farmer drives a plow through it. Someone digs a well, a grave, a foundation.
Someone else kneels and plants a rose, or pours fragrant oil on it at a shrine. Rain pounds it. Children run on it.
And through all of it, the earth holds everything up and grows whatever is put into it. It doesn't sulk at the plow or preen at the perfume. Guru Arjan saw a portrait of a person in that.

teach.h: THE WIND ON KING AND BEGGAR.
teach.b: After the lotus and the sun, the stanza adds a third picture: the brahm giaanee looks on all alike, as the wind blows the same on king and beggar. Raaj is the king, rank the poorest of the poor.
The wind doesn't check who it's touching. Then the fourth: brahm giaanee kai dheeraj ek.
The God-conscious one has one, steady patience, jio basudhaa, like the earth. Basudhaa is an old name for the earth.

Kou khodai, kou chandan lep: one person digs it, another anoints it with sandalwood paste, and the earth is the same to both. Sandalwood paste is what you'd smear on something precious, something honored.
So the picture stretches as far as it can: one person tears into you, another honors you, and you don't change. It's not saying the earth doesn't notice the plow.
It's saying the earth doesn't become a different earth depending on who's standing on it. That's dheeraj, patience, steadiness.
The stanza closes with a last picture: this is the brahm giaanee's quality, the way it is fire's natural nature to burn. Not forced. Just what fire is.
Lotus, sun, wind, earth, fire: every picture is nature doing what it does, the same for everyone. Equal treatment, flowing from who you are, not from who's in front of you.

how: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a picture of steady, equal treatment of everyone, an ideal also lived in the gurdwara, where all sit and eat together as equals.

o: the wind that blows on everyone

games.q: like the earth — tap the pairs.
p: an old name for the earth

s: the earth picture means not noticing who hurts you
the earth isn't a different earth depending on who stands on it.
the stanza pictures the wind blowing the same on king and beggar
the brahm giaanee looks on all alike.
every picture in this stanza comes from nature
lotus, sun, wind, earth and fire.

games.q: one person digs into the ground; another anoints it with sandalwood. what does the earth do?
o: gives more to the one with sandalwood.
games.why: jio basudhaa kou khodai kou chandan lep: the God-conscious one's patience is like the earth's.

practice: Think of two people you'll meet today, one who usually treats you well and one who doesn't, and notice how your body changes as you picture each, opening for one, bracing for the other.
Then feel your weight on the floor and picture yourself as the ground under both of them, steady, holding, the same. Breathe out, and let both faces rest on you equally.

wordCard.voice: Basudhaa, the earth. Dug by one, anointed with sandalwood by another, and the same to both.
